newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia gas monopoly seeks billions on West markets.
newsitem.headline: Russia gas monopoly seeks billions on West markets.

text.p: The world's largest natural gas company, Russia's secretive RAO Gazprom, will jump into Western capital markets and raise $2 billion to $3 billion within six months, one of its bankers said Monday.

Gazprom has mandated Dutch bank ABN-Amro and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs to arrange an issue of at least $1 billion in Eurobonds and another $500 million to $1 billion in convertible bonds, ABN-Amro's Russia manager Frank Kuijlaars told Reuters.

Gazprom, the target of young Russian government reformers and tax collectors seeking about $2.5 billion in back taxes, will also look for $500 million to $1 billion in short-term bridge financing within the next month, ABN-Amro officials said.

"Gazprom would like to receive proceeds from these issues, at least partially, earlier than it can go to the market," ABN-Amro managing board member Jan Maarten de Jong told bankers, explaining the need for bridge financing.
He said Gazprom and the banks had "more or less" finalised a mandate for the package on Friday.
Gazprom's local financial adviser said the $2 billion to $3 billion project was being planned but declined to comment further.

Gazprom's entrance into the Eurobond market of company and sovereign debt issued outside a debtor's country and chiefly in non-native currency, could be larger than the Russian Federation's own debut last year.
The Eurobond will be at least $1 billion, the size of Russia's first post-communist bond, and will be issued, along with convertible bonds, within six months, Kuijlaars said.
The gas monopoly controls virtually all Russia's natural gas pipelines, produces 95 percent of its gas and is building a multi-billion dollar pipeline known as the Yamal to Europe.
But the announcement comes as Gazprom is trying with mixed success to woo foreign investors and deal with a reformist government that intends to control the 40 percent stake it owns.

Gazprom American Depositary Shares (ADSs), the only approved form of foreign investment in Gazprom, have seen almost none of the gains of leading Russian shares, an index of which gained 75 percent in the first two months of the year alone.
But the ADS, which was launched last October at $15.75 and covers 10 underlying shares, is almost three times as expensive as the price of the local shares it covers.
On Monday the ADS traded at $17.50 at midday in London against 67 cents for shares on the Russian Trading System.
ABN-Amro officials did not give details of the convertible bond, such as whether it would convert into an ADS.

Gazprom Chairman Rem Vyakhirev, who recently called foreigners who tried to buy shares on the local market "swindlers," has begun to court foreigners playing by its rules, inviting current Western investors to tour its facilities.
It is trying to increase transparency, including instituting Western-standard accounting this year.
